190.title: No one can purify another (161–166)
190.hook: by oneself evil is done, by oneself one is purified
190.carry: no one can do it for you
190.howItsDone: Buddhists honor teachers, monastics and spiritual friends as essential guides, while holding, as this verse says, that each person must do the work of purifying their own mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, first yourself: set yourself right, then teach. Your line was self is lord of self.

Someone can drive you to the gym. They can buy you the shoes, set the alarm, even stand next to you on the treadmill cheering. But they can't do your push-ups for you. If they do fifty, your arms stay exactly as they were. Everyone knows this about the body. We're less sure about it with the mind. We'd love for someone to hand us calm, or patience, or a clean conscience, already assembled. Chapter twelve ends with a verse that gently shuts that door.
screen: `THEY CAN DRIVE YOU TO THE GYM.` → `THEY CAN'T DO YOUR PUSH-UPS.` → `CALM, ALREADY ASSEMBLED?`

segments.voice: Verse one sixty-three, in Max Müller's words: "Bad deeds, and deeds hurtful to ourselves, are easy to do; what is beneficial and good, that is very difficult to do." No sugarcoating. Just before it, verse one sixty-two pictures great wickedness as a creeper that drags down the tree it wraps around. Then the heart of it, verse one sixty-five: "By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another." The Pali word for purity is suddhi: cleanness, clearness. The verse is careful and balanced: harm and its undoing, both in your own hands. That's sobering, and some readers find it freeing too: impurity, the verse says, belongs to oneself as well. Then verse one sixty-six, with a story. The commentary says that when the Buddha announced he would pass away in four months, many monks crowded around him anxiously. One monk, Attadattha, stayed away and meditated instead. The others complained. Asked why, he said he wanted to reach the goal while the Buddha was still alive, and the Buddha praised him: this is how to honor me. Don't neglect your own good for another's, the verse says. That doesn't mean you walk alone. Teachers and friends matter a great deal on this path. But they're the ones driving you to the gym.

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been waiting for someone else to fix in you: being less anxious once work calms down, or kinder once your family is easier. Ask what one step you could take yourself, however small; not the whole journey, one step. Then take the step that's already in your hands: this breath, then this one.
Suddhi. Purity, cleanness: verse one sixty-five's teaching that by oneself harm is done, by oneself one is purified, and no one can purify another.
Your line: no one can do it for you. Others can guide; the work itself stays in your hands. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: A bubble, a mirage (167–171)
191.hook: look on the world as a bubble, as a mirage, and the king of death won't see you
191.carry: real for a moment, never solid
191.tomorrow: The moon from behind a cloud (172–178)
191.howItsDone: Buddhists across many schools reflect on impermanence with images like the bubble, the mirage and the dream, often in chanting or in teachings given at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suddhi: by oneself harm is done, by oneself one is purified. Your line was no one can do it for you. Today, chapter thirteen begins: the world.
screen: `NO ONE CAN DO IT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Blow a soap bubble on a sunny day and watch it. For a second or two it holds the whole world on its skin: the sky, the trees, your own stretched face, swirling in rainbow colors. It's real. And then, with no sound at all, it's gone. Or drive a highway in summer heat toward the shimmering pool on the road that never gets any closer. Real shimmer, no water. Chapter thirteen of the Dhammapada hands you those two sights as glasses to see through.
screen: `A SOAP BUBBLE IN THE SUN.` → `WATER ON THE HIGHWAY THAT ISN'T.` → `TWO SIGHTS TO SEE THROUGH.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with a wake-up call, verse one sixty-eight: "Rouse thyself! do not be idle! Follow the law of virtue!" The commentary says the Buddha spoke it when he first came home to his father's city and walked the streets with his alms bowl. His father, the king, was mortified to see his son begging, and hurried to stop him. The Buddha answered that going for alms was the custom of his lineage, the lineage of Buddhas. Then today's line, verse one seventy: "Look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage: the king of death does not see him who thus looks down upon the world." In Pali, a bubble is pubbuḷa, and a mirage is marīcikā. Neither is nothing. A bubble really shimmers; a mirage really shines. They just aren't solid or lasting. That's the way of looking the verse asks for: not that the world doesn't matter, but that nothing in it will hold still or hold your weight forever. And its promise is plain: the king of death does not see the one who looks this way. Verse one seventy-one adds a picture: the world is like a glittering royal chariot; fools sink into it, the wise don't cling. A Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, closes with a list of similes in the same spirit, among them a dream, a bubble, dew and lightning. Two very different texts, one shared image.

segments.voice: If you can, look at something that shimmers, bubbles in a glass of sparkling water, light on a window, your reflection in a dark screen; if not, picture one soap bubble floating in front of you, and watch its colors move without trying to catch it. Then close your eyes and watch your thoughts the same way: each one shimmering, real for a moment, then gone with no sound.
A bubble. Verse one seventy: look upon the world as a bubble, as a mirage: shining, real for a moment, never solid.
Your line: real for a moment, never solid. A worry that feels huge is a bubble too. See you tomorrow.

192.title: The moon from behind a cloud (172–178)
192.hook: one who was careless and becomes earnest lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds
192.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often point to Aṅgulimāla's story and these verses to encourage people to begin again after lapses, and lay Buddhists retake the precepts regularly as a fresh start.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bubble: look upon the world as a bubble, as a mirage. Your line was real for a moment, never solid.

Three weeks of sitting every morning. Then a trip, a cold, a hard week, and suddenly it's been ten days. Here's the odd part: the stopping was easy. It's starting again that's hard, because starting again means admitting you stopped, and that can feel embarrassing enough that some people simply never do. Even the moon disappears for a while behind clouds, and nobody thinks less of it when it comes back.
screen: `THREE GOOD WEEKS, THEN TEN DAYS.` → `STARTING AGAIN IS THE HARD PART.` → `EVEN THE MOON DISAPPEARS.`

segments.voice: Verse one seventy-two, in Max Müller's translation: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Reckless here means heedless, careless, the opposite of the earnestness from chapter two. The verse doesn't say the careless past vanishes. It says the person, now awake, gives light. Verse one seventy-three goes further: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." The old commentary attaches this verse to a turnaround the early texts tell in full: Aṅgulimāla, the bandit who wore a garland of his victims' fingers, who met the Buddha, stopped, became a monk, and was remembered as having reached awakening. If the moon can come out from behind that cloud, the story seems to ask, which cloud is too thick? The Pali word for moon here is candimā, and the picture is simple: the moon sliding free of a cloud, and suddenly you can see the road. The chapter ends with a striking claim, verse one seventy-eight: "Better than sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all worlds, is the reward of the first step in holiness." The first step: in the tradition, the moment one first truly enters the stream of the path. Not the finish line. The first step, and the second beginning, and the third.
screen: `RECKLESS, THEN SOBER.` · `DEEDS COVERED BY GOOD DEEDS.` · `AṄGULIMĀLA'S TURNAROUND.` · `THE FIRST STEP OUTSHINES EMPIRES.` · then, large: `THE MOON COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: Think of one practice you've let slip, sitting, a precept, a kindness you used to do, exercise, a call you used to make, and notice any little cloud of embarrassment around it, without pushing it away. Picture the moon behind a thin cloud, and the cloud slowly drifting on. Then begin again, right now, in the smallest way: this breath counts, this sit counts.
Candimā. The Pali word for the moon: one who was careless and then became earnest lights up the world, like the moon freed from clouds.
Your line: the moon comes out. Beginning again needs no apology and no ceremony. That's day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: Hard to be born human (179–182)
193.hook: hard is it to be born human, hard the life of mortals, hard to hear the true teaching
193.howItsDone: Many Buddhist traditions, Theravada and Tibetan alike, begin practice by reflecting on the preciousness and rarity of a human life, often using the Buddha's image of the blind turtle and the yoke.

segments.voice: Yesterday, candimā: the careless one who turns earnest gives light, like the moon freed from clouds. Your line was the moon comes out. Today, chapter fourteen begins: the Buddha.

It's a Tuesday. You woke up, found the coffee, checked the weather, and went through the usual list of complaints. And yet: you woke up. You have a mind that can wonder about its own life. You're hearing words first spoken twenty-five centuries ago that still reached you. None of that feels rare, because it happens every day. One verse in chapter fourteen turns this ordinary Tuesday over to show the price tag.
screen: `AN ORDINARY TUESDAY.` → `YOU WOKE UP.` → `THE PRICE TAG ON A DAY.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens by praising the Awakened One as trackless: no desire can lead him anywhere, so there's no trail to follow him by. Verse one eighty-one says the gods envy those who are awake. Then verse one eighty-two, in Max Müller's words: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals, difficult is the hearing of the True Law, difficult is the birth of the Awakened." In Pali, each line begins with the same word, kiccha: hard, difficult, rare. Hard to be born human. Hard to live as a mortal. Hard to hear the true teaching. Hard for a Buddha to appear at all. Four rarities stacked up, and you're standing on all four. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha gives a picture of how rare. Imagine a yoke with a single hole, tossed on the ocean and blown about by the winds. Once every hundred years, a blind turtle rises to the surface. What are the chances it puts its head through that hole? That, he says, is how rare it is for a being who has fallen into the lower realms to come back to a human birth. You don't have to hold the Buddhist view of many lives to feel what this verse does. It takes the thing you complain about every morning and shows you it's a winning ticket. Buddhists hear it as urgency, not guilt: this life, with a mind that can learn and a teaching within reach, is the rare chance. The list of complaints can stay; it just doesn't get the whole day.
screen: `THE TRACKLESS ONE.` · `KICCHA — HARD, RARE.` · `A BLIND TURTLE AND A YOKE.` · `A WINNING TICKET, NOT GUILT.` · then, large: `THIS LIFE IS RARE.`

segments.voice: Go through this ordinary day slowly: you're breathing, rare; you can hear, rare; someone, somewhere, you love or who loves you, rare; food, a roof, a moment to sit, not everyone has these; a teaching you're thinking about, rare. Don't force gratitude; just let each ordinary thing be seen once, the way you'd look again at something you almost threw away. Then rest in this one rare breath.
Kiccha. Hard, difficult, rare: verse one eighty-two says rare is human birth, rare a mortal life, rare the hearing of the teaching, rare the arising of a Buddha.
Your line: this life is rare. Even on a Tuesday. Day one hundred ninety-three, done.

194.title: The teaching of all Buddhas (183–187)
194.hook: not to do any evil, to do good, to purify one's mind: this is the teaching of the awakened (Dhammapada 183)
194.howItsDone: Verses 183–185, known as the Ovāda Pāṭimokkha, are chanted in Theravada monasteries, and many Buddhists commemorate their teaching on Magha Puja, the full moon of the third lunar month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kiccha: four rarities, and a blind turtle surfacing through a yoke. Your line was this life is rare.

Could you sum up everything you believe in one sentence? Most of us would ramble, or give a slogan we don't quite live by. Some traditions have a short answer ready, a line people can say in one breath. In Buddhism, today's verse is that kind of line: this, it says, is the teaching of all the Awakened. It's short enough to memorize by the end of today. And it's so hard that, the story goes, an old man can't manage it.
screen: `EVERYTHING IN ONE SENTENCE?` → `A LINE SAID IN ONE BREATH.` → `SHORT, AND HARD.`

segments.voice: Verse one eighty-three, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Three movements. Avoid harm. Do good. Purify the mind. The first two are about what you do. The third turns inward: in this verse, it isn't enough to behave well; the mind behind the behavior has to be cleared, of greed, of hatred, of confusion. That's what sitting is for. Tradition holds that this verse, with the two after it, was spoken on a full-moon day to twelve hundred fifty awakened disciples who gathered without being called. Remember Magha Puja, from camp three? This is the teaching that holy day remembers. Verse one eighty-four adds the spirit of it: "The Awakened call patience the highest penance." Not dramatic self-punishment. Patience. Verse one eighty-five lists small, practical pieces: "Not to blame, not to strike," to eat in moderation, to sit in solitude, to dwell on the highest thoughts. People in China tell a story about this verse. A famous poet-official climbed to meet a Chan master who lived in a tree, and asked for the essence of Buddhism. The master gave him this verse. The poet laughed: a child of three knows that. The master answered: a child of three may know it, but an old man of eighty can't do it. The teaching is simple enough to say, and big enough for a lifetime.

segments.voice: Avoid: is there one small harm, a jab, a shortcut, a bite of gossip, you can simply not do today? Do: is there one small good, a greeting, a thank-you, a helping hand, you can add? Purify: that one happens right here, as the breath settles the mind and each flicker of irritation or wanting is noticed and let pass, like dust settling in a glass of water.
Sāsana, the Pali word for teaching: verse one eighty-three says not to do any harm, to do good, to purify one's own mind.
Your line: avoid, do, purify. The whole teaching of the Buddhas fits on three fingers. Until tomorrow.

195.title: The real refuge (188–196)
195.hook: frightened people run to mountains, groves and shrines; the safe refuge is the three jewels and the four truths
195.howItsDone: Buddhists across the world take refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, reciting the formula three times in Pali or their own language, at ceremonies, at the start of practice and often daily at a home shrine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sāsana: avoid harm, do good, purify the mind. Your line was avoid, do, purify.

Where does your mind run when you're scared? For some it's the fridge. For some it's the phone, scrolling until the feeling goes numb. For some it's work, or a person, or a plan with seventeen backups. Plenty of us have a hiding spot, and it works, for about an hour. Then the fear comes back and finds us there. Chapter fourteen closes with a list of places frightened people run to, and then a different kind of shelter.
screen: `WHERE DOES YOUR MIND RUN?` → `THE FRIDGE, THE PHONE, THE PLAN.` → `IT WORKS FOR ABOUT AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Verse one eighty-eight, in Max Müller's words: "Men, driven by fear, go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees." And one eighty-nine: "But that is not a safe refuge, that is not the best refuge." The verse isn't mocking anyone's shrine; Buddhists themselves honor the tree the Buddha sat beneath. Its point is about fear: a place can't carry you out of pain. Then verse one ninety: "He who takes refuge with Buddha, the Law, and the Church". That's Müller's Victorian English for three Pali words: Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, the awakened teacher, the teaching, and the community that practices it. Buddhists call them the three jewels. Müller's Church is the Sangha: the community of monks and nuns, and in a wider sense, for many Buddhists, everyone walking the path. And the refuge isn't only in who you trust but in what you see. Verse one ninety-one names it: the four noble truths, in Müller's words, "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain". Seeing those clearly, verse one ninety-two says, is the safe refuge, the best refuge. You met the refuges on day one hundred twenty-three, as a practice. In Pali the line runs Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, I go to the Buddha for refuge, then the same for the Dhamma and the Sangha, three times through; others say it in Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese or English. Saraṇa means shelter, protection. Not a cave to hide in. A place to stand.
screen: `MOUNTAINS, FORESTS, SACRED TREES.` · `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `THE FOUR TRUTHS, SEEN CLEARLY.` · `SARAṆA — A PLACE TO STAND.` · then, large: `THE REAL REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Name, without judging, one place you run to when you're afraid, then sit with the three refuges: the awakened one, the possibility that a human mind can wake up; the teaching, the way things really are, pain and its causes and its ending; the community, the people who have walked, and are walking, this path beside you. If you're Buddhist, you can quietly say the refuge line, Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi; if not, simply rest in whichever of the three feels most like solid ground.
Three jewels. The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, the teacher, the teaching and the community, named together as the true shelter from fear.
Your line: a place to stand. Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and the four truths seen clearly. Day one hundred ninety-five, and counting.

196.title: Among those who hate (197–200)
196.hook: let us live happily, not hating those who hate us; owning nothing, we feed on joy like the bright gods
196.howItsDone: Verses from the chapter on happiness are often chanted and quoted by Buddhist teachers as a picture of the monastic ideal: owning little, living on alms, and staying free of hatred in hostile surroundings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the real refuge: not mountains or groves, but the three jewels and the four truths. Your line was a place to stand. Today ends the week, and chapter fifteen begins: happiness.

There's an office where everyone complains. The coffee's bad, the boss is worse, and the group chat is one long sigh. Or the family dinner where two relatives haven't spoken civilly in years. You walk in cheerful, and within twenty minutes you're grumbling too. Moods travel. So is it even possible to be happy in a room like that, without faking it and without joining in? Chapter fifteen of the Dhammapada says yes, four times in a row.
screen: `THE OFFICE WHERE EVERYONE COMPLAINS.` → `TWENTY MINUTES, AND YOU'RE GRUMBLING.` → `HAPPY IN A ROOM LIKE THAT?`

segments.voice: Verse one ninety-seven, in Max Müller's translation: "Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!" Then the same shape again: happy and free of illness among the ill, free of greed among the greedy. The Pali opens with sukha, happiness, ease, the opposite of dukkha. The old commentary gives these opening verses a setting. Two clans, the Buddha's own Sakyans and their neighbors the Koliyans, shared a river, and in a dry season they were ready to go to war over its water. The Buddha stood between them and asked which was worth more, water or the lives of warriors. They put down their weapons. Then the fourth, verse two hundred: "Let us live happily then, though we call nothing our own! We shall be like the bright gods, feeding on happiness!" The commentary says this was spoken on a day the Buddha went for alms and came back with an empty bowl. Owning nothing, fed by joy. The bright gods, in Buddhist cosmology, are radiant beings said to feed on joy. On this view, happiness doesn't depend on the room agreeing with you. It depends on the room not getting inside. A fitting end to the week. No one can purify another. A bubble, a mirage. The moon from behind a cloud. This life is rare. Avoid, do, purify. The real refuge. And today: we live happily, even among those who hate.
screen: `SUKHA — EASE, HAPPINESS.` · `TWO CLANS AND ONE RIVER.` · `AN EMPTY BOWL, FED BY JOY.` · `A WEEK, TO HAPPINESS.` · then, large: `WE LIVE HAPPILY.`

segments.voice: Picture a room you'll be in today that tends to be grumpy, a meeting, a commute, a kitchen, and see yourself walk in neither pretending to be cheerful nor joining the sighing: just steady, like a lamp set down in a dim room, a little warmth in your chest. If someone there is hostile, wish them ease for one breath: may you be free from this. Then let the room go, and rest.
Sukha. Happiness, ease, the opposite of dukkha: verse one ninety-seven says let us live happily, not hating those who hate us, free from hatred among the hating.
